I’m 73 years old and I’ve farmed this 3.1 mu plot in Quzhou for 40 years. My wheat went into the ground last October after I ploughed the field and put down base fertilizer — that’s how I’ve always done it. Now it’s spring, the wheat is waking up, and I need to manage it through to harvest in June. I have a well on my land, so I can irrigate when I need to, which matters because the rain here doesn’t always come when you want it. My son works in a factory in the city, but he comes back to help during busy times like harvest. For the wheat this year, I’ll top-dress nitrogen at the jointing stage — about 15 kg per mu of urea. I won’t go crazy with phosphorus and potassium; maybe 5 kg and 3 kg per mu, since the soil has built up some fertility over the years. I’ll irrigate three times: once when the wheat is jointing, once at heading, and once during grain filling. Two sprays should be enough — a herbicide in early spring and one fungicide or insecticide if the weather turns humid. I expect around 500 kg per mu if things go normally. After I cut the wheat in early June, I’ll plant maize right away — you can’t waste time in the double-crop system. I’ll use hybrid seeds from the shop; the yield is much better than the old varieties. I’ll run the rotary tiller quickly after wheat harvest to prepare the seedbed, then sow. Base fertilizer goes in at planting, and I’ll side-dress more nitrogen when the maize reaches the big trumpet stage. Three irrigations for maize — jointing, silking, and filling. Two pesticide applications: one for weeds and one for corn borers or aphids if they show up. I expect about 600 kg per mu for the maize. I don’t follow every new trend the extension agents talk about. At my age, I stick to what works. My land is small, so I manage it carefully. The key is timely irrigation and not letting weeds or pests get out of hand.
